enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (40 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organization (12 marks); Expression (16 marks); Accuracy (12 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write on from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. You should write between 450 - 500 words. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity.

questions.enonce_markdown: **b)** Describe a market scene on the eve of an important festival.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: Mbouda market at dawn, two days before the Christmas and New Year festival.
2. Sights and sounds: traders, goods, colours, music and calls.
3. Smells and people: food stalls, bargaining, crowded lanes, children and thieves.
4. Conclusion: the closing of the market at night and the feeling of expectation.

**Model composition (499 words)**

On the eve of the Christmas festival, the Mbouda market is the busiest place in the whole division. By five o'clock in the morning, long before the sun has climbed over the hills, the road leading to the market is already crowded with buyers, porters and trucks loaded with goods. I once went there with my mother, and what I saw that morning has remained fresh in my memory.

The first thing that strikes a visitor is the noise. Traders shout the prices of their goods at the top of their voices. "Fresh tomatoes, three hundred francs a heap!" cries a young woman, while a man selling second-hand shoes beats an empty tin to attract customers. From a small shop at the corner, loud makossa music pours into the lane, and every few seconds a motorbike taxi blows its horn and forces the crowd to part like a river around a rock.

The next thing is the colour. Rows of stalls display bright wrappers, new shirts, shining plastic buckets and toys of every shape. Mountains of oranges, pawpaws and pineapples glow in the early light, and baskets of red peppers sit beside heaps of green vegetables. Children press their faces against the stalls selling sweets and balloons, begging their parents to buy something special for the festival.

Then come the smells. In the food section, women fan charcoal fires under big pots of boiling plantains, while others turn pieces of roasted fish and sizzling suya over the flames. The sweet smell of doughnuts mixes with the sharp smell of fresh fish and the rich aroma of palm oil. My stomach began to rumble as soon as we entered that lane.

The lanes themselves are so narrow and so full that one can hardly walk. Shoppers push and squeeze against one another with heavy baskets on their heads. Bargaining goes on everywhere. "Mama, I will give you two thousand," says one customer. "Two thousand? You want me to lose my business?" replies the seller with a laugh, and after a long argument they settle on two thousand five hundred. Meanwhile, a loudspeaker warns people to beware of pickpockets.

By late afternoon, the traders began to sell the last of their goods at lower prices, and the crowd grew even thicker. Tired mothers dragged their children by the hand, men carried goats on their shoulders and boys pushed wheelbarrows loaded with bags of rice. Everybody wanted to finish shopping before the evening.

At sunset, the market slowly began to empty. Traders folded their tents, counted their money and tied up what remained of their goods. The ground was covered with rubbish, banana peels and torn paper. Yet in spite of their tiredness, the faces of the people were bright with happiness. Tomorrow would be the festival, and each family was returning home with food, new clothes and hope. That evening I understood that the market was not merely a place for buying and selling, but the beating heart of our community.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organization | 12 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 16 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 12 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Telling a story instead of describing a scene (the topic asks for a description).
2. Describing only what is seen: good descriptions also use sounds, smells and the feelings of the people.
